title: Review: mechanics of mycelium materials
abstract: Abstract The biological growth of fungal root structure, called mycelium, can be engineered to develop innovative fibrous and biocomposite materials. Mycelium materials have potential as sustainable alternatives to petroleum-derived materials for load-bearing applications. To realize this potential, there is an increasing effort dedicated to understanding the mechanics of mycelium materials. This work presents a systematic review of our current understanding of the mechanics of mycelium materials with a specific focus on structure–property relationships. The review first explores how the mycelium’s fiber network structure varies depending on whether it is grown as a two-dimensional (2D) membrane, a cellular foam, or as a matrix embedding biomass particles or a 3D-printed substrate. The mechanical behavior under tension and compression for three types of mycelium materials (i.e., membranes, foams, and composites) is discussed. The review showed that mycelium membranes exhibit nonlinear stress–strain behavior due to their dense and highly connected 2D fiber network, whereas mycelium foams behave like a bending-dominated soft solid due to their 3D porous structure. The composite mechanics is dominated by the densely packed structure of substrate particles and 3D-printed substrate geometry. Multi-scale modeling approaches for predicting mycelium mechanics are presented. A comparative analysis of the mechanical property space is presented to reveal that mycelium membranes show the higher stiffness and strength compared to other two materials due to their higher density. This review summarizes how microstructural features affect deformation and failure mechanisms of mycelium materials as well as highlights important knowledge gaps, providing a strong foundation to advance the field. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The detrimental impacts of petroleum-derived, non-degradable, and emission-intensive materials (e.g., plastics) on our environment, health, and non-renewable energy supply are driving the critical need for their sustainable alternatives. Biological matters, abundantly available in nature and capable of forming materials without complex processing, provide opportunities for sustainable material development. The engineering of biological living matters has emerged as a prominent paradigm in contemporary materials design. Considerable research efforts have focused on developing novel materials from diverse natural resources, such as bacteria [ 1 ], cellulose [ 2 ], silk proteins [ 3 ], and eggshell [ 4 ]. In this context, the vegetative tissue of fungi that forms the root-structure (called mycelium) has been explored extensively over the last decade to develop a wide variety of materials, including thin films [ 5 ], foams [ 6 ], and composites [ 7 ]. Mycelium materials exhibit a unique combination of properties that are highly tunable based on fungal biology, material chemistry, and hierarchical microstructure, providing a versatile biological platform for sustainable material engineering.

The building block of mycelium is the filamentous cells of fungi, called hyphae [ 8 ]. Hyphae grow as tubular or ribbon-like fibers with micron-sized diameters depending on the species and growth environment. Hyphae grow in length from a tapered region at their tips called the extension zone. The growth is driven by the osmotic flow of water from the hyphal cell wall to the external environment due to the higher concentration of solutes within the hyphae than in the external environment. It generates large internal hydrostatic pressure, which allows hyphae to penetrate their feeding substrate and extract nutrients by enzymic activity [ 9 ]. The hyphal cell wall is primarily composed of chitin, β-glucans, and proteins [ 10 ,  11 ]. The outer surface is enriched with β-glucans, which function as a mucilaginous layer, while the inner region consists of chitin microfibrils covalently cross-linked with other polysaccharides, including glucans [ 10 ,  11 ]. This hierarchical organization endows the hyphae with structural integrity, where chitin microfibrils play a dominant role in providing mechanical rigidity and strength [ 12 ,  13 ].

Hyphae have strong branching ability, crucial for their growth through rapid exploration of nutrition sources [ 14 ]. Hyphal branching creates fractal tree-like mycelial colonies [ 15 ]. Hyphal fusion (anastomosis) joins neighboring colonies, providing the mycelium a fiber network-like microstructure [ 16 ]. The branching density and network topology are largely controlled by hypha type. Hyphae can exhibit three specific types in terms of branching. They are called generative, skeletal, and binding hyphae [ 8 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 ]. The generative hyphae grow as highly branched fibers, primarily responsible for producing spores. Skeletal hyphae are mostly unbranched and axially elongated fibers. Binding hyphae are highly branched and short fibers that act as physical cross-links to bind other hyphae. Mycelium can exhibit distinct network topologies, depending on whether it consists of a single type of hyphae (monomitic), two types of hyphae (dimitic), or all three types of hyphae (trimitic) [ 20 ]. Fungal species largely control hypha type and network topology of mycelium.

The biological growth of mycelium has been leveraged to develop functional materials using two distinct mechanisms. The first mechanism involves processing of the as-grown mycelium to develop two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) fibrous materials. This class of materials is called pure mycelium materials [ 21 ]. Several researchers developed mycelium-based 2D microporous membranes with attractive material properties, including hydrophobicity [ 5 ], self-healing ability [ 22 ], super-amphiphilicity [ 23 ], and cellular biocompatibility [ 24 ]. These material properties are not intrinsic to all types of mycelium, rather they depend on fungal species, growth conditions, post-processing, and functionalization of mycelium membranes with additives. These membranes have potential applications in filtration [ 23 ,  25 ,  26 ], tissue engineering [ 24 ], and textiles [ 27 ]. Mycelium-based 3D fibrous materials provide flexible foam-like properties useful for packaging and energy absorption applications [ 6 ]. The second mechanism focuses on developing composite materials by growing mycelium on particulate substrates or 3D-printed solid substrates. Mycelium cohesively embeds the substrate particles within its fibrous matrix during the growth phase, naturally forming a composite material after the living organism is deactivated. This class of mycelium composites is referred to as particulate composites in this article although the particle size and shape vary among different studies. In case of 3D-printed substrates, mycelium forms a dense fibrous skin on the surface of the substrate. This class of mycelium composites is called 3D-printed composites in this work. The biological growth process of fungal mycelium has been explored extensively to develop biocomposites with various lignocellulosic substrates [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 ]. The as-grown composites, without chemical additives or post-processing, are entirely biodegradable after end-of-life and sustainable due to their growth-driven fabrication with minimal fossil fuel input. Mycelium composites have applications in construction [ 30 ,  37 ], packaging [ 7 ], architecture [ 38 ], thermal insulation [ 39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ], and water treatment [ 44 ].

Significant research effort has been dedicated to mycelium materials over the last decade. Several review articles have summarized different aspects of mycelium materials, including fabrication [ 45 ,  46 – 47 ], material function [ 21 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ], and applications [ 27 ,  47 ,  51 ,  52 ]. However, the mechanics of mycelium materials received less attention in these studies. An in-depth understanding of their mechanical behavior is critical to expanding the viability of mycelium materials for multidisciplinary applications. For example, mycelium materials have high separation efficacy, but they cannot sustain the high pressure of filtration processes (e.g., reverse osmosis) due to low strength [ 23 ]. They can mimic foam mechanics under compression, but their stiffness and strength are inferior to the rigid foams used in energy absorption applications (e.g., helmets) [ 53 ].

Within this motivation, this work presents a comprehensive review of the mechanics of mycelium materials based on the progress made over the last decade. The review is focused on pure mycelium materials and their composites with agricultural biomass substrates. The discussion begins with an overview of fabrication protocols and the resulting microstructures of various mycelium materials. This is followed by a review of their mechanical behavior under tensile and compressive loading. The fundamental link between the mycelium’s fibrous microstructure and the emergent mechanics has been discussed using the well-documented literature on the mechanics of fiber networks, providing novel insights into the structural basis of the mechanical response of specific types of mycelium materials. Finally, an analysis of the mechanical property space is included to highlight the key parameters governing the mechanics of mycelium materials.

sections.heading: 2D membrane
paragraphs: Mycelium-based 2D membranes are fabricated by exploiting the natural growth of mycelium in direct contact with its nutritional source. Two distinct fermentation techniques have been developed in the literature depending on whether the nutrition medium is in liquid or solid state (Fig.  1 ). In liquid fermentation, fungal spores or mycelial fragments are inoculated into a sterile aqueous medium (e.g., potato dextrose broth) containing carbon, nitrogen, and mineral nutrients [ 5 ,  54 ]. Hyphae grow by apical extension and branching in the liquid media and self-assemble into a planar fiber network at the air–liquid interface. In contrast, solid-state fermentation uses a solid gel-like media, most commonly agar, to grow the mycelium membrane [ 55 ,  56 ]. Agar is a polysaccharide extracted from seaweeds with a sugar-based skeleton that is capable of thermal gelation. The transformation of randomly coiled polymer chains of agar into an entangled network of double helices on cooling forms the gel structure [ 57 ]. The agar gel is supplemented with nutritional ingredients (e.g., glucose, malt extract, and yeast extract) to support hyphal growth [ 56 ,  58 ]. In contact with a solid nutrition medium, some hyphae grow in a planar direction along the gel surface (called ‘surface hyphae’) while some hyphae penetrate the gel to extract nutrients (called penetrative hyphae) [ 59 ,  60 ]. In addition, some hyphae grow upward from the gel surface into the air (called aerial hyphae). The presence of aerial hyphae leads to higher thickness in membranes fabricated by solid-state fermentation [ 55 ]. Figure 1 Schematics of the fermentation system of mycelium membranes using  a  a liquid media and  b  a solid media. The corresponding macro-scale membranes are shown in ( c ) and ( d ), respectively, and their fibrous microstructures are shown in ( e ) and ( f ), respectively. Figure panels  c ,  e  are adapted from ref. [ 54 ]. Figure panels  d ,  f  are adapted from ref. [ 5 ].

Microstructures of liquid fermented mycelium membranes exhibit a double-layered architecture. The liquid-facing (“floating”) side is composed of flat and intertwined hyphae, while the air-exposed (“aerial”) side exhibits a highly branched hyphal network with characteristic diameters in the order of 1 µm (Fig.  1 e) [ 22 ]. In addition to hyphal fibers, the membranes can also contain other developmental structures [ 61 ]. Membranes fabricated by solid fermentation exhibit less heterogeneous and purely fibrous microstructure, consisting of tube or ribbon-like hyphal fibers (Fig.  1 f). The air-exposed surface is generally more fibrous than the surface in contact with the gel media [ 23 ].

sections.heading: Cellular foam
Particulate composite
paragraphs: Mycelium-based particulate composites consist of biomass substrate particles cohesively embedded in the biologically grown fibrous matrix of fungal mycelium. Figure  3 a shows a typical fabrication process of mycelium composites reinforced with corn stover particles [ 31 ]. The composite fabrication involves inoculating a bag of nutritionally supplemented corn stover particles with fungal tissue, followed by an incubation period to allow fungal colonization of the substrate particles. High lignocellulosic content of biomass particles enables hyphal growth and hyphae-particle interfacial bonding in this stage. Next, the colonized substrate is homogenized through mechanical grinding and mixed with additional solid nutrients. The homogenization step is used to break down the mycelium colonies and minimize the spatial density fluctuation of the mycelium matrix in the composites. The mixture is grown in molds of desired shapes for several days, which is oven-dried to end the hyphal growth and obtain the final composite. Several researchers also developed modified fabrication techniques, which directly grow mycelium in the molds or without the homogenization step being mixed with substrate particles in single step. This generic fabrication protocol has been used for different types of substrates, including hemp, cotton, cellulose, corn stover, wood chips, sawdust, and natural fibers [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 ,  37 ,  66 ]. Figure 3 a  Fabrication process of a mycelium-based particulate composite that involves (i) inoculation of biomass particles (corn stover) with mycelial tissue, (ii) inducing mycelial colonization of substrate particles, (iii) followed by growth in a rectangular mold to obtain desired shape, and (iv) heat treatment to kill living tissue in a convection oven.  b  Macro-scale structure of final composite,  c  a cut section of the composite.  d  a zoomed view of the cut-section showing the interfacial bonding between mycelial matrix (white) and substrate particles (brown), and  e  a scanning electron micrograph of the composite showing a substrate particle embedded in the fibrous matrix of mycelium. Adapted from ref. [ 31 ].

The final composite retains its molded shape, as shown by the macroscopic specimen in Fig.  3 b. Cross-sectional views (Fig.  3 c and 3d) reveal a heterogeneous internal architecture in which biomass particles (brown) are embedded within the mycelial matrix (white). At higher magnification, the SEM image (Fig.  3 e) shows that individual substrate particles are physically entangled within the dense fibrous network of the mycelium matrix. It indicates that mechanical rigidity arises from the hyphal growth-mediated discrete interfacial bonding between particles and the mycelium matrix [ 31 ]. This is distinct from traditional particle-filled polymer matrix composites, where the particle–matrix interface is continuous and adhesive in nature [ 67 ].

sections.heading: 3D-printed composite
paragraphs: 3D-printed mycelium composites are fabricated using extrusion-based and direct-ink-writing additive manufacturing techniques [ 35 ,  36 ,  68 ,  69 ]. The fungal spores, nutrient ingredients, and substrate particles are mixed with a viscoelastic material with suitable rheological properties to obtain a viscous mixture that is extrudable and has shape-retention ability. Typically, biopolymers such as agar, alginate, chitosan, and xanthan gum are used as rheological modifiers to aid printability [ 35 ,  68 ,  70 ,  71 ]. The mixture is supplemented with malt, psyllium husk, and peptone as nutritional elements, whereas spent coffee ground is commonly used as the substrate [ 35 ,  36 ,  72 ]. As illustrated in Fig.  4 a, a customized 3D printer comprising a large material reservoir, a motor-driven plunger, and an auger-based printhead is employed to extrude the mixture through a nozzle and form a 3D structure through layer-by-layer deposition. This configuration of the 3D-printer decouples material storage from deposition, reduces flow resistance, and allows precise control over extrusion rate during printing. This approach enables the formation of self-supporting structures without the use of molds, as shown in Fig.  4 b. The 3D-printed structure acts as a substrate for fungal inoculation and incubation, allowing the growth of fungal mycelium both over the surfaces (Fig.  4 c) and in the pores of the 3D-printed porous structures [ 68 ,  69 ,  73 ]. The major advantage of this approach is that it is not limited to relatively simple shapes as achieved through the mold-based growth process. The open configuration of the 3D-printed structures facilitates the effective growth of mycelium by ensuring uniform air supply [ 36 ]. This method also provides a high-throughput approach for printing large-scale structures [ 74 ]. Figure 4 a  Schematic of a 3D-printing system used for fabricating mycelium composites. The primary raw material is a viscous fluid, primarily composed of coffee grounds, which is 3D printed, and it serves as the substrate for mycelium growth.  b  a zoomed view of the 3D-printed substrate.  c  Progression of mycelial colonization of the substrate over time. Left to right: freshly printed substrate, 5 days of mycelial growth, and 10 days of mycelial growth. Adapted from ref. [ 35 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical behavior in tension and compression
2D Membrane
paragraphs: The mechanical behavior of mycelium membranes has been studied in uniaxial tension using dog-bone specimens (Fig.  5 a). The membranes exhibit toe-heel-linear stress–strain behavior (Fig.  5 b) as commonly observed for materials with fiber network-like microstructures [ 75 ]. The membrane’s fibrous microstructure also undergoes rapid reorganization under uniaxial tension (Fig.  5 c). The toe regime occurs at low strain (1–3%), in which the membranes exhibit very low effective stiffness due to initial random organization of hyphal fibers. This regime is characterized by the bending deformation of wavy fibers to straighten up and reorient along the loading direction. This regime is also affected by the slack in the specimen. Theoretical studies on the mechanics of random fiber networks showed that the degree of fiber waviness controls the transition from toe to heel regime. Networks with a higher degree of fiber waviness transitions to the heel regime at larger strain [ 76 ]. The heel regime, also known as transition regime, involves progressive recruitment of hyphal fibers to support the tensile loading. In this regime, the stress–strain curve exhibits strain stiffening as more fibers (i.e., hyphae) become aligned in the loading direction [ 75 ]. Figure 5 a  A representative tension testing specimen of mycelium membranes, adopted from ref. [ 61 ].  b  Representative stress–strain curves of mycelium membranes as-grown with different fungal species-  Ganoderma lucidum  (solid line) adopted from ref. [ 24 ] , Pleurotus ostreatus  (dash-dot line) adopted from ref. [ 24 ], and  Aspergillus nidulans  (dashed line) adopted from ref. [ 61 ].  c  Schematics of membrane’s fibrous microstructural evolution with increasing strain.

Next, the stress–strain curve becomes linear due to the formation of long chains of aligned fibers (Fig.  5 c). Most of the load is carried by these long chains, and the membrane ruptures without further structural change after this stage. It is noted that most studies report membrane stiffness as the slope of this linear regime. Interestingly, no stress softening is observed beyond the maximum stress points in the stress–strain curves of mycelial fiber networks, suggesting hyphae break in a brittle fashion without significant plastic deformation or damage (Fig.  5 b). This is distinct from metal and electrospun polymer fiber networks, which exhibit stress softening and yielding under uniaxial tension due to plastic deformation of fibers [ 77 ,  78 – 79 ].

The nonlinear mechanics of mycelium membranes strongly depends on the fungal species. Figure  5 b shows the stress–strain curves of membranes obtained from three species-  Ganoderma lucidum, Pleurotus ostreatus, and Aspergillus nidulans.  The  Ganoderma lucidum  membrane transitions from toe to hill regime at lower strain and undergoes stronger strain stiffening than the  Pleurotus ostreatus membrane  [ 24 ] .  In contrast, the  Aspergillus nidulans  membrane exhibits a softer response than the other two species, but much higher failure strain [ 61 ]. These mechanistic differences are associated with variations in network structure, hyphal diameter, and cell wall chemical composition among the three species. For example,  Ganoderma  species generally exhibits a highly branched network of thin hyphae [ 80 ] .  It contains lower porosity than  Pleurotus  species [ 24 ] .  The microstructure of  Aspergillus nidulans  shows a relatively sparse hyphal network with embedded developmental cells, which is responsible for the weak nonlinearity observed in the stress–strain response properties [ 61 ] .

The mechanical behavior of mycelium membranes is also sensitive to the nutritive composition of the feeding substrate. Haneef et al. (2017) showed that the addition of potato dextrose broth improves ductility of the membranes by stimulating the production of plasticizers (lipids, proteins) in the hyphal cell wall [ 5 ]. High malt content of the substrate enhances the membrane stiffness and strength due to the formation of more branched and dense hyphal fiber network in contact with a sugar-rich substrate [ 56 ]. In addition to substrate composition, multiple studies showed genetic modification as a viable strategy to tune membrane microstructure and alter mechanical behavior. Gary et al. genetically altered the microstructure of  Aspergillus nidulans  to enhance fibrous hyphal content, and it also improved the mechanical properties of the membranes [ 61 ]. Appels et al. also showed that genetic modification of mycelium can dramatically improve the mechanical properties by increasing mycelium density in the membranes [ 81 ]. This is because it transforms the fibrous and porous microstructure of the membrane into a solid, film-like microstructure [ 81 ]. Post-treatment of as-grown membranes can also be used to control the mechanical behavior of mycelium membranes. For example, glycerol-based treatment of mycelium membranes transforms a stiff and brittle membrane into a soft and ductile one, where the mechanical properties strongly depend on the concentration of glycerol [ 82 ]. Mycelium membranes also exhibit self-healing ability after post-treatment with malt extract agar (MEA)-rich solution due to hyphal regrowth in presence of additional nutrition [ 22 ].

sections.heading: Cellular foam
Particulate composite
paragraphs: Mycelium-based particulate composites exhibit distinct mechanical behavior compared to mycelium-based membranes and foams (Fig.  7 ). In uniaxial tension, the composites behave like an elastic–plastic material with a well-defined linear elastic regime and yield point. Unlike the mycelium foam, they exhibit gradual strain softening after the yield point until the failure point (Fig.  7 a), suggesting progressive damage accumulation in the material. The ductility is also very weak, such that the composites fail prematurely at low strain (1–5%) without significant plastic deformation. Damage in mycelium composites under tensile loading occurs at the microscopic level of the hyphal fiber network. The crack initiates through the breakage of hyphal fibers in the weakest domain of the fiber network, which propagates gradually with increasing strain by breaking neighboring hyphae. When a substantial number of hyphal fibers are broken, the micro-scale crack transitions into a macro-scale crack that runs through the composite cross-section to cause permanent failure. The interfacial debonding of substrate particles also contributes to the composite failure under tensile loading [ 32 ,  88 ]. In general, mycelium matrix, especially the dense outer skin, provides elasticity to the composites, while the plasticity results from the particulate substrate [ 28 ,  73 ]. Figure 7 Representative stress–strain curves of mycelium-based particulate composites under  a  tension and  b  compression.  c  Deformed configurations of a mycelium-based particulate composite at increasing levels of compressive strains corresponding to the points (I-V) in ( b ). Data in  a  is for a hot-pressed mycelium composite with rapeseed straw as the particulate substrate, adopted from ref. [ 28 ]. Data in  b – c  is for a corn stover particle-filled mycelium composite, adopted from ref. [ 31 ].

Brittleness is a ubiquitous feature of mycelium composites in tension. Appels et al. showed that mycelium composites fabricated with different fungal species ( Pleurotus ostreatus  vs.  Trametes multicolor ) and substrates (straw, sawdust, cotton) exhibit similar brittle behavior [ 28 ]. Hot or cold pressing of the composites improves composite modulus and strength due to a reduction in internal porosity, but cannot enhance ductility. Elasker et al. studied the effect of substrate hybridization through the addition of organic (bacterial cellulose) and inorganic (nanoclay) particles [ 89 ,  90 ]. While substrate hybridization improves the internal bond strength of the composites, the overall effect on the tensile strength and ductility is minimal [ 49 ].

Toughness of mycelium composites under tension is significantly lower compared to mycelium mats and foams. This is linked to the heterogeneous microstructure of the mycelium matrix (i.e., hyphal fiber network) in the composites largely due to spatial fluctuation of fiber density. Due to non-uniform density distribution, the failure occurs in regions of lowest fiber density prematurely, leading to lower toughness of the composite [ 91 ]. The mycelium matrix heterogeneity is linked to the geometry of substrate particles, which cannot be controlled precisely since they are derived from agri-waste feedstock. Islam et al. (2018) showed that the size of corn stover particles can vary over a broad range (1 to 10 mm) in the mycelium-based particulate composites despite sorting the particles through mesh sieving [ 31 ]. Elsacker et al. (2019) studied mycelium-based particulate composites with natural fiber-based substrates where the particle size also had a broad distribution (5 to 25 mm) [ 29 ]. The non-uniform size and shape distributions of particles affect the mycelial growth homogeneity and continuity by creating spatial gradients in porosity, pore size, and oxygenation [ 36 ]. It induces local density fluctuations of the hyphal fiber network from the surface to the core in the composites [ 28 ,  31 ,  92 ]. The hyphal fiber network structure is also altered during the grinding step of the fabrication process to transfer the colonized substrate from the bag to the plastic molds. While this step is necessary to obtain the desired shape of the final composites, it can dramatically change the microstructure by creating several sub-networks with embedded particles that interconnect during the secondary growth phase of hyphae [ 93 ]. It critically affects the fiber–fiber connectivity and local fiber density of the hyphal fiber network, which are critical geometric parameters that dictate the elastic and failure behavior of random fiber networks [ 83 ,  94 ,  95 ].

The tensile mechanical behavior of mycelium composites is further affected by the entanglement-induced load transfer between the discrete particles of substrate and the mycelium matrix. The particle–matrix bonding is expected to be much weaker in mycelium composites than traditional particulate polymer matrix due to the non-continuum, fibrous nature of the matrix phase. The microstructural heterogeneity of the matrix and packing density of particles also affect the interfacial bonding between hyphae and particles. The particles loosely entangled with the mycelium matrix do not contribute to the composite mechanics as expected, and their percentage cannot be predicted in priori.

The compression stress–strain response of mycelium-based particulate composites exhibits two distinct regimes: a linear elastic regime and a rapid strain-stiffening regime (Fig.  7 b). The linear elastic regime occurs due to the elastic bending deformation of hyphal fibers while being compressed between substrate particles. The effective modulus of the composite (slope of the linear elastic regime) is proportional to the matrix density or volume fraction. The presence of a dense matrix skin provides a significantly large linear elastic limit up to 10–20% strain. For composites with a high-volume fraction of substrate particles and a relatively sparse matrix, this regime represents a roughly horizontal stress–strain curve with nearly zero modulus [ 73 ]. The size distribution of substrate particles minimally affects the composite response in this regime [ 31 ]. Interestingly, the transition from the linear elastic regime to the stiffening regime occurs without any intermediate softening regime as commonly observed in foam-like materials [ 96 ]. The presence of particles prevents global buckling instability of the fibrous mycelium matrix. Figure  7 c shows the deformed configuration of a mycelium composite at different levels of compressive strains. It is observed that the mycelium matrix locally collapses due to excessive buckling of hyphal fibers, but the collapsed regions cannot percolate the entire cross-section due to the presence of stiff particles in the vicinity [ 31 ].

The strain stiffening regime is associated with the densification of substrate particles at large compressive strain. The stress increases rapidly with strain due to the formation of particle–particle contact points and the gradual increase of contact pressures. Since the effect of mycelium matrix is negligible in this regime, the stress–strain response of the mycelium composites in this regime mimics the compression response of randomly packed particles, which can be approximated by a power law [ 83 ,  97 ,  98 ]. Similar to mycelium foams, mycelium composites exhibit strong hysteresis and Mullins effect under cyclic compression primarily due to matrix viscoelasticity and frictional interaction of particles [ 31 ]. Due to viscoelasticity, they can recover a portion of plastic deformation after being compressed [ 99 ]. Mycelium composites can generally withstand large compression (40–60%) without stress softening or disintegration of particles from the composites [ 31 ,  32 ,  73 ]. However, composite specimens with a large aspect ratio (i.e., height-to-width ratio) can undergo failure under compression, especially for a high volume fraction of particles [ 100 ]. The slenderness of the specimens induces excessive buckling deformation, which leads to the formation of surface cracks and progressive damage of the materials under compression [ 101 ]. Failure can involve different modes, including protruding failure mode or shear failure mode [ 30 ].

sections.heading: 3D-printed mycelium composite
paragraphs: The mechanical behavior of 3D-printed mycelium composites is largely dominated by the substrate properties. In tension, the composites exhibit a brittle response such that the material fails at low strain, immediately after the linear elastic regime (Fig.  8 a). The failure is associated with the delamination of the 3D-printed layers of the substrates [ 35 ,  36 ,  70 ]. Interestingly, mycelial colonization leads to lower tensile properties of the composites than uncolonized substrates. It is attributed to the living mycelium’s digestion of organic components (e.g., cellulose) in the substrate, which reduces the bulk density or solid fraction of the 3D-printed substrate leading to reduced tensile properties [ 35 ,  36 ]. The infill density of 3D-printed substrates also minimally affects the overall mechanical properties of the composites [ 36 ]. On the other hand, the compression response shows three distinct regimes, like foam materials. First, a linear elastic regime is observed, which is dominated by the elastic deformation of the dense 3D-printed substrate and mycelium matrix. The formation of dense mycelium matrix surrounding the substrate enhances the compressive modulus of the composites [ 68 ]. Next, a plateau regime is observed with fluctuations in stress due to the yielding and buckling instability of the composite. Finally, substantial compaction of the composites (> 50%) causes a rapid rise in stress with strain. Unlike tensile response, mycelial colonization enhances the composite toughness (area under the stress–strain curve) in compression compared to an uncolonized substrate, suggesting mycelium acts as a reinforcing matrix to distribute the stress evenly throughout the material and prevent permanent failure [ 35 ]. Figure 8 Representative stress–strain behavior of a 3D-printed mycelium composite under  a  tension and  b  compression. Data in  a – b  are adapted from ref. [ 35 ].

sections.heading: Computational modeling
paragraphs: Mycelium materials are multiscale materials in which the constituent size varies over a broad range from micrometer to millimeter length-scale. Pure mycelium materials have two essential length scales. The first scale is associated with the fiber network of hyphae at the microscale. The hyphal network density can also vary on an intermediate scale between the micro and meso scales. For the mycelium composites, an additional length-scale occurs due to the substrate particles ranging in size from hundreds of microns to mm. Given these multi-scale complexities, there are limited studies on the modeling of mycelium materials. Only one research group presented a multi-scale modeling framework (Fig.  9 ) for mycelium materials based on the finite element (FE) method [ 31 ,  53 ]. Figure 9 Schematic representation of the multiscale modeling procedure of mycelium materials  Adapted from ref. [ 31 ]

Pure mycelium materials:  Discrete fiber network models were used at the micro-scale to represent the mechanical behavior of fibrous mycelium as a function of the effective network density. The network structures were constructed using the Voronoi tessellation algorithm [ 83 ], in which the geometric properties (e.g., hypha diameter, segment length, and pore size) were calibrated from microscopy images of mycelium [ 53 ]. The density fluctuation was incorporated in a meso-scale continuum model by introducing subdomains. Each subdomain has a distinct density (sampled from an experimentally calibrated distribution), and its constitutive behavior is derived from the microscale network model of the corresponding density through an empirical hyperelastic formulation [ 53 ]. The cyclic softening behavior was captured by introducing a phenomenological model in the continuum representation. The multi-scale model predictions were validated using both tension [ 6 ] and compression [ 53 ] experiments.

Mycelium composites:  A particle-filled composite FE model was developed to simulate the mechanical behavior of mycelium-based particulate composites under compression [ 31 ]. The mycelium matrix was represented as a homogenized continuum phase, and its constitutive behavior was defined based on the two-scale model of pure mycelium materials. The biomass particles (e.g., corn stover) were represented as randomly distributed inclusions with linear elastic behavior, and their assembly was generated using a dynamic FE simulation-based particle packing algorithm [ 102 ]. The composite model provided two key insights into the mechanics of mycelium composites. First, it was observed that the composite response is dominated by the matrix phase at the small strain. The matrix softens at larger strains due to its foam-like properties, while the composite stiffens due to the formation of contact interaction among substrate particles. Second, the particle size and aspect ratio have minimal effect on the composite mechanics due to the random organization of particles [ 31 ].

The computational modeling framework of Islam et al. (2018) is a powerful tool to guide design and parameter optimization for diverse mycelium materials with different types of particulate substrates and hyphal network structures [ 31 ]. For example, the discrete fiber network model can provide mechanistic insights into how generative, skeletal, and binding hyphae contribute to the hyphal network mechanics. It can also elucidate how hyphal cross-section (ribbon vs. cylindrical) and branching density affect the macro-scale mechanical behavior of mycelium materials [ 103 ]. The composite model can be leveraged to understand the effects of particle mechanical properties, spatial arrangement within the matrix, and packing density. Future work should also consider more advanced techniques to address the limitations of current models. First, advanced models are required to account for plastic deformation and rupture of hyphal failure. This can be achieved by incorporating a damage criterion in the constitution model of hypha in the fiber network model [ 104 ]. Second, the composite model assumes that the substrate particles are perfectly bonded to the matrix, whereas in actual composites, the particles are simply entangled within the fibrous matrix of mycelium. The particle–matrix interfacial debonding is also not incorporated into the model. Therefore, the model cannot predict damage or failure behavior of mycelium materials, especially under tension loading. This would require explicit representation of particle–matrix interfacial bonding in the model, as done in a recent study on a fiber network model with embedded spherical particles [ 105 ]. Future work should also consider uncertainty in model parameters by adopting probabilistic approaches like stochastic finite element modeling [ 106 ]. It is important because the properties of mycelium materials are highly sensitive to growth conditions.

sections.heading: Effect of bulk density
Effect of process parameters
paragraphs: It is well-recognized that the mechanical properties of mycelium materials strongly depend on the processing parameters. While the effects of process parameters have been extensively studied for mycelium composites, literature on parametric studies of mycelium foam and membranes is limited. Therefore, we reviewed here the parameters controlling the mechanical properties of mycelium composites. Specifically, we focused on the effects of three key parameters, namely substrate type, fungal species, and pressing, on the mechanical property space of mycelium composites. Compression data of mycelium composites from Fig.  10  is re-plotted in Fig.  11  as a function of substrate (Fig.  11 a) and fungal species (Fig.  11 b). The open symbols represent non-pressed composites, whereas filled symbols represent hot or cold pressed composites. Data is plotted as modulus vs strength to highlight the synergistic effects of parameters on both properties. Figure 11 Effect of substrate type and fungal species on mechanical properties of mycelium-based composites. Data is presented as Young’s modulus vs strength plots as a function of  a  lignocellulosic biomass substrates and  b  fungal species. The open symbols represent non-pressed composites, and the filled symbols represent pressed composites. Data is adopted from refs. [ 5 ,  28 ,  30 ,  33 ,  66 ,  73 ,  93 ,  115 ,  119 ,  120 ].

The effect of fungal species on the mechanical property space of mycelium composites is shown in Fig.  11 b. Mycelium composites are predominantly fabricated using three common species:  Pleurotus ostreatus, Ganoderma lucidum,  and  Trametes multicolor. P. ostreatus  has a monomitic hyphal network, composed mainly of generative hyphae. In contrast,  G. lucidum  and  T. multicolor  have trimitic hyphal networks, consisting of all three types of hyphae (e.g., generative, skeletal, and binding hyphae) .  In general, fungal species with trimitic and dimitic hyphal networks show a higher growth rate than those with monomitic networks, leading to a higher bulk density of the matrix [ 113 ,  114 ]. Trimitic networks also lead to thicker fungal skin on the composite surface compared to monomitic networks [ 28 ]. Despite these structural differences, the mechanical property space, as a function of fungal species, exhibits a more narrow and round shape than the space associated with substrate (Fig.  11 a). For example, Aiduang et al. fabricated mycelium composites with several Ganoderma species and three distinct substrates. They found that the mechanical properties vary significantly with substrate type, but vary minimally as a function of fungal species [ 113 ]. It indicates that the presence of different types of hyphae has a weaker effect on the modulus and strength of mycelium composites. The overall network density of the fibrous mycelium matrix is the major parameter that controls the composite mechanical properties from the perspective of fungal species.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook
paragraphs: This work presented a systematic review of the mechanical behavior and properties of different types of mycelium materials in close connection to their fibrous, hierarchical, and heterogeneous microstructures. It was demonstrated that it is possible to achieve highly nonlinear and distinct mechanical behavior in different types of mycelium materials. Mycelium membranes exhibit a biopolymer-like strain stiffening response under tension due to their 2D fiber network-like microstructure, which can also be modulated by fungal species. Mycelium foam behaves like an elastic–plastic polymer material with high flexibility and energy absorption capacity under cyclic compression due to its 3D interconnected microporous structure. Mycelium-based particulate composites can withstand large compression without instability as well as dissipate energy under cyclic loading. The analysis of mechanical property space revealed that mycelium membranes provide higher stiffness and strength than the other two types, primarily due to higher bulk density. The mechanical properties of mycelium composites are more sensitive to substrate type than fungal species due to reinforcement potential of stiff biomass particles. Since the structure is determined by the biological growth of fungal mycelium, the mechanical differences observed are inherently dependent on several factors associated with fungal growth conditions. Clearly, the current understanding of mycelium material mechanics is incomplete and although significant progress has been made over the last decade, more work is needed to effectively control the mechanical properties of mycelium materials for target applications. In closure, it is imperative to highlight critical knowledge gaps that require further investigation to advance the field: Mechanical properties of substrate particles:  Mycelium composites are fabricated using a wide variety of plant-based and woody biomass particles as the substrate, but the mechanical properties of these biomass particles are rarely characterized in most studies. A detailed understanding of biomass particles’ stiffness and strength as a function of their feedstock origin is necessary to ensure they will function efficiently as reinforcing fillers for the composites. Hyphae-particle interfacial mechanics:  Composite mechanics strongly depends on the interfacial bonding between hyphae and biomass particles. The substrate particles loosely entangled with the hyphal network contribute minimally to the composite stiffness and strength. There exists a compelling need to better understand the interfacial mechanics of mycelium composites as well as strategies to improve the bonding strength through surface functionalization of biomass particles. Computational and data-driven modeling:  Advanced computational models are required to predict the deformation mechanisms of mycelium materials, including but not limited to rupture of individual hyphae, interfacial debonding of particles, and pressing-induced deformation of mycelium materials. Data-driven and machine-learning (ML) models will also be useful to interpret the complex interrelations between large sets of process parameters affecting the mechanics of mycelium materials.
